rationale: Last round crashed only because it wrote into the read-only `DataFrame.values` view. This round keeps the same hypothesis and builds the standardized matrix in a fresh writable NumPy array. Each study has its own sequencing depth and protocol, so the plan is to log-transform genus abundances (pseudocount scaled to each sample's depth) and z-score every genus within its study. That should let the pooled random forest learn shared IBD shifts, such as loss of Faecalibacterium/Roseburia and gain of Enterobacteriaceae, instead of study-specific thresholds. The change is untested and has no Dev score yet.

The four studies sequenced different 16S regions, so the same organism is often assigned to a genus in one study and left at family or order level (`g__;`) in another. Genus-only features therefore break up shared IBD signals such as Enterobacteriaceae gain or Lachnospiraceae/Ruminococcaceae loss. This round keeps the genus features exactly as in the current best and adds summed relative abundances at the phylum, class, order and family levels, so the random forest can split on coarser taxa that every study classifies the same way. I haven't run it, so it has no Dev score yet.

Lower alpha diversity is one of the most consistent IBD findings across studies, but genus-level relative abundances only capture it indirectly. This round adds a few alpha-diversity features: Shannon and inverse Simpson at OTU and genus level, plus OTU richness rarefied to 1,000 reads. I compute the rarefied richness as an exact expected value rather than by random subsampling, so it is deterministic and less sensitive to sequencing depth, which differs between studies. The genus features and the random forest are unchanged.

Case/control ratios differ a lot between the four studies, so the pooled forest can partly learn "which study is this" as a stand-in for disease. That shortcut is useless when AUROC is scored within each study. I'll reweight the training samples so cases and controls carry equal total weight inside every study. This makes study independent of the label in the training distribution, so the trees have to split on IBD-related taxa. Features and the forest are otherwise unchanged; I haven't run this yet, so it has no Dev score.

Many genera show up in only one study, either because of that study's 16S region or protocol, or because they are rare noise. The forest can still split on them, but those splits mostly encode study identity or noise rather than a shared IBD signal. I'll keep only genera that are present in at least 10% of samples in at least two training studies. The filter uses only study ids from the training metadata, never labels, so the forest should concentrate on taxa that every study can measure, such as Faecalibacterium, Roseburia and Enterobacteriaceae genera.

This round adds a second model alongside the random forest. Microbiome composition is log-ratio data, and a regularized linear model on CLR-transformed shared genera captures smooth, additive dysbiosis gradients that tree thresholds handle poorly, such as Faecalibacterium/Roseburia loss and Enterobacteriaceae gain. I'll rank-average its predictions with the current RF; the logistic model uses the same study×class weights, and its regularization strength is tuned only by grouped inner CV on the training fold.

Within-study AUROC doesn't change when a constant offset is added to the linear model's scores inside a study. Per-study offsets in the CLR features are therefore pure batch noise that distorts how the logistic regression estimates its coefficients. I'll centre each study's CLR genus profile on its training-fold mean, with cases and controls weighted equally, and apply the same centre to that study's test samples. The coefficients should then be learned from within-study IBD contrasts rather than between-study protocol shifts. Unlike round 2's per-study z-scoring, this only shifts feature values and only touches the linear model; the RF is unchanged.

Right now the RF and CLR-LR scores are rank-averaged over the whole pooled test fold, so how much each model counts inside a study depends on how its scores interleave with samples from other studies. The metric is within-study AUROC, so I'll rank each model's scores within each test study (normalized to [0,1]) before averaging. Each model then has equal, study-independent weight in every within-study ordering. Ranking within a study is monotone, so each model's own within-study AUROC is unchanged and study is used only to harmonize, not as a predictor. I haven't run this, so it has no Dev score yet.

I'll tune the random forest's leaf size and per-split feature fraction by grouped inner cross-validation, scored as within-study AUROC to match the harness metric. Fully grown trees on a pooled, batch-heavy dataset tend to fit study-specific quirks, so larger leaves or wider feature sampling should make the forest's rankings smoother and more transferable. That should also blend better with the CLR logistic model; the LR and the feature pipeline are unchanged. I haven't run this, so it has no Dev score yet.

All OTUs without a genus call are currently merged into one `g__` feature. That bin mixes unclassified Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcaceae, which are lost in IBD, with unclassified Enterobacteriaceae, which gain in IBD and are often not resolved to genus by 16S. Pooling them cancels opposite signals. This change assigns each OTU to its deepest named rank instead (genus if named, otherwise family, order, and so on), so unresolved taxa keep their family- or order-level identity in both the random forest and the CLR logistic model.

Right now the RF and the CLR logistic regression are blended 50/50 regardless of how well each does. I'll choose the RF weight from {0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 0.65, 0.8} by grouped inner CV on the training fold, scored as within-study AUROC. The inner predictions come from the forest that was already tuned there plus five cheap logistic refits at the chosen C. The hypothesis is that one model ranks samples better than the other in this pooled data, and a data-chosen weight should beat a fixed one. The grid excludes 0 and 1, so both models always contribute. I haven't run this, so it has no Dev score yet.

I'm adding one literature-derived feature to both the random forest and the CLR logistic model: the Gevers 2014 microbial dysbiosis index. It is the log of summed IBD-increased families (Enterobacteriaceae, Pasteurellaceae, Veillonellaceae, Fusobacteriaceae, Neisseriaceae, Gemellaceae) over summed IBD-depleted taxa (Erysipelotrichaceae, Bacteroidales, Clostridiales). I compute it from all OTUs, including those with no genus call. Family and order labels are assigned consistently across 16S regions, so this single score should carry the shared IBD shift across studies in a way that scattered genus columns do not.

The CLR logistic model currently chooses C by pooled inner-CV AUROC. Because case/control ratios differ by study, pooled AUROC rewards whichever C best tracks study identity. I'll tune C by grouped inner CV scored as within-study AUROC, the harness metric, as round 10 already did for the forest. The chosen C should then favour coefficients that rank samples well inside each study.

I'm adding a third model to the RF + CLR-logistic rank average: a shallow, heavily regularized LightGBM on the shared genera, using the same study×class weights. Boosting fits the residual errors left by earlier trees, so it should pick up taxon interactions and threshold effects that the bagged forest and the additive linear model both miss. Its number of boosting rounds is chosen by grouped inner CV scored as within-study AUROC, and the three models are rank-averaged with equal weight. This is untested and has no Dev score yet.

I'm changing the CLR logistic model from pure L2 to elastic net (saga), with the L1 ratio picked from {0, 0.5, 1} together with C by the same grouped inner CV. Most of the ~150 shared genera probably carry study-specific batch noise. The idea is that a sparse penalty keeps the few markers that shift in every study, such as Faecalibacterium/Roseburia loss and Enterobacteriaceae gain. Because 0 is in the grid, it can still fall back to the current L2 model. This is untested, so it has no Dev score yet.

I'll add ExtraTrees configurations to the forest grid that is already tuned by grouped inner CV on within-study AUROC, so inner CV picks between a bagged RF and ExtraTrees and their leaf sizes. ExtraTrees draws split thresholds at random instead of optimising them, so it can't latch onto study-specific abundance cutoffs, which come from depth, 16S region and protocol differences. Its smoother ranking should transfer better across the four studies and blend better with the CLR logistic model. This is untested and has no Dev score yet.

I haven't run this change, so it has no Dev score yet. Standardizing CLR features puts genera found in only two of the four studies on the same scale as genera found everywhere, so the logistic model may give weight to study-specific batch signal. I'll choose how strict the logistic model's genus filter is (detected in ≥2, ≥3 or all 4 training studies) by the same grouped inner CV that already picks C. The forest keeps its current ≥2-study filter, since tree splits are less affected by uninformative columns.

The four studies were sequenced to very different depths, so a genus's zero-or-not pattern and the CLR pseudocount (currently half of each sample's smallest nonzero value) both mostly reflect sequencing depth, i.e. batch. This change sets a common detection limit: genus relative abundances below L, which is 1 over the training-fold 10th-percentile read depth, are set to zero, and the CLR model uses one fixed pseudocount 0.5·L for every sample. Zeros and log-ratios then mean the same thing in every study, for both the forest and the logistic model.
